items.title: VirusTotal’s New Ransomware Detection Catches Malware Missed by All 75 Antivirus Engines
items.summary: VirusTotal has rolled out a ransomware detection update that checks whether suspicious files actually encrypt user documents during execution. The new checks caught a Python ransomware sample that recorded zero detections across 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis, showing how behavior checks can expose threats that static scanning misses. The update spans VirusTotal and Google Threat Intelligence, adding verified encryption tags, stricter ransomware behavior rules, and support for real-time hunting. Rather than treating encryption code or heavy file activity as proof of ransomware, the system looks for damage to user documents inside controlled test environments. The new tag:encrypts-files search tag and behaviour_tags:encrypts_files behavior trait work across CAPE Sandbox and Zenbox on Windows, plus macOS Mirage on Apple Silicon. VirusTotal introduced macOS Mirage to provide native Apple Silicon malware analysis and detailed behavior reports. High-level overview of CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage verifying file encryption before tagging T1486.(source : virustotal ) Each environment contains realistic user documents. During and after execution, the sandboxes inspect changed files for broken document structures, unusual byte patterns, and higher data randomness. These checks examine the results on disk instead of relying only on calls to operating system encryption tools. VirusTotal Ransomware Detection Missed That approach covers malware using built-in AES, ChaCha20, XOR, or partial encryption routines. Such variation matters because ransomware families use different methods to damage files, as seen in Beast ransomware’s partial encryption design . The sandboxes also track linked file reads, writes, renames, and deletions. The sandbox excludes routine installer activity, browser caches, and temporary files. A ransom note or encryption function alone does not trigger the tag. The standout example is system_update.pyw, a Python locker linked to a .k404 extortion campaign submitted on November 17–18. Although its static scan showed 0/75 detections, Zenbox observed it running through pythonw.exe, deleting itself, and rewriting Desktop documents into .k404 encrypted files. Undetected Python locker encrypts Desktop files with the .k404 extension (T1486) (source : virustotal ) A related Windows program, K404T_Fidye.exe, had 10/75 detections. Another locker, lkd.exe, had just 3/75. CAPE confirmed that both encrypted user documents, providing evidence beyond their antivirus scores. The checks also identified INC Ransom encrypting documents.INC files and dropping INC-README.txt ransom notes. INC has previously appeared in healthcare attacks linked to Vanilla Tempest , underlining the value of clear encryption evidence during investigations. VirusTotal reports that the tag matched 55 files among 328,257 newly submitted unique files analyzed since November 17. Manual review found no benign software among those matches. These early results do not establish that future scans will have no false positives. CAPE also tightened its mapping to MITRE ATT&CK T1486, Data Encrypted for Impact. Generic file activity now requires verified document encryption before receiving that mapping. VirusTotal says the change reduced false-positive T1486 volume across the platform by 97.6%. INC Ransom encrypts user files with the .INC extension (T1486 ) (source : virustotal ) Analysts can search entity: file tag:encrypts-files or use VirusTotal Livehunt with the YARA-X trait vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES for real-time alerts. Adding a low antivirus detection threshold helps focus hunts on overlooked samples. A missing tag, however, is not a clean verdict. Malware may need passwords, user input, network access, or more time before it starts encrypting. The feature confirms observed file encryption, not the absence of ransomware when a sandbox run shows none. Analysts should also remember that the reported 0/75 score describes the sample at analysis time, not a permanent detection result, and does not prove every endpoint product would fail to stop it. items.title: The Patch Fear Trap: Why We Still Fear the Fix More Than the Exploit in 2026
items.summary: W arning : this blog is another experiment. The idea for a blog came from a repeat conversation I had many, many times over the years. The content is researched, debated, refined, “hardened” by a Gemini skill I created (using Gemini 4 Argon). Then Claude Fable 5.2 performed a peer review, and refined the text. Then Gemini 4 Neon looked at it and lamented “Claude staccato” style and rewrote in what it considers “Anton voice.” And then I edited it, and cut out some iffy stats AIs shoved in. Let me know if this sucks, and I will stop. Promise! Earlier this year, I kicked off my Patch Sound Barrier series by arguing that AI-driven exploit development is accelerating while legacy remediation speed is stuck with organizational “physical” limits. In Part 2 and in the 15-minute patch post , we looked at the machinery needed to remediate at a somewhat similar rate. Yet when I talk to security and IT leaders in late 2026, we keep hitting a stubborn human reality: people delay patches because they fear the patch breaking production more than the exploit . And, yes, recent incidents like the now-notorious FAA router disruption remind everyone that outages frequently happen during routine updates. In essence, they are not truly wrong. “Routine” (ha!) maintenance still triggers massive operational headaches across sectors: classified networks dropping offline, consumer platforms failing post-update, and officials reassuring the public that outages were “just routine updates” rather than cyberattacks. That is the point — routine updates are scary as hell to some people and thus those people believe they have good reasons for not remediating security flaws. Meanwhile, the exploit clock has gone negative. Mandiant’s M-Trends 2026 puts mean time-to-exploit at negative seven days — exploitation begins (in some cases!) before the vendor fix arrives. (I remember hearing “patch management is a solved problem ” back in 2006. It wasn’t.) The short takeaway: you cannot cure patch fear by yelling louder about AI exploits and threat actors. ”OMG CVSS 10 WE ARE ALL GONNA DIE” will not change the mind of a CIO who just spoke with a peer whose patch went bad a week before. To the admin on call, an exploit is a probabilistic rumor with shared blame, while a broken patch is an immediate outage with their name on the change ticket. “Attackers might hack us, but YOU will break production” is not cured by showing scarier threat intelligence. Gemini psychoanalyzes patch fears What may help? Patch fear is rational, not a culture problem. How rational? Think about fear of snakes vs. fear of flying: one is a rational reaction to an immediate physical threat in front of you; the other is an irrational phobia of a statistically safe system. So in 2026, is a security patch a plane or a snake? Snake vs plane Security teams often treat patch hesitation as a lack of “security culture” — or like a fear of flying that can be cured with more threat intel slides. It isn’t. To the sysadmin holding the pager, an untested Tuesday patch on a fragile server is a rattlesnake on the trail. It is a rational response to asymmetrical personal risk. Here is how the same vulnerability ticket looks from the two sides of the building: Table of fears Until recently, I assumed this table is very past looking, but it is definitely the present for many. Still, nobody gets fired for waiting for the change window. People do get fired for taking down production at 2 PM. As long as both statements are true, lectures about scanner queues are just noise. So yes, in 2026, admins who distrust brand-new updates have real evidence on their side. And here is the uncomfortable 2026 twist: AI didn’t just speed up the exploit clock; it degraded vendor patch quality too. Under pressure to beat negative time-to-exploit, vendors are shipping rushed point fixes while attackers point LLMs at patch diffs the hour they drop to find bypasses. According to Terra Security’s late-2026 study of published CVEs and advisories, the share of security fixes failing or requiring a follow-up patch within 90 days jumped 11.5x in 2026 (from 0.2% to 2.3%) — and bugs with bypassed fixes were 4x more likely to land on CISA’s KEV list. Do the compounding math (0.977¹⁰⁰): if you push 100 distinct updates a quarter, a 2.3% per-patch failure rate gives you a 90.25% quarterly certainty of stepping on at least one vendor-supplied landmine. Waiting 72 hours so you aren’t the vendor’s unpaid crash-test dummy isn’t laziness then. Soaking a patch in canary deployment makes sense, but waiting is only valid if: You are mitigated while you wait. Leaving exposed assets unmitigated for 14 days isn’t caution — it’s unmanaged risk today. [I am working on a general purpose mitigation framework to be revealed soon] You actively test in canaries. Passive waiting relies on others to find bugs. Your canary rings are the only test suite that matters for your stack. Rule of thumb: wait on the patch binary if you must, but never leave the risk unmitigated. Every decision to delay a patch must come with an associated mitigation decision that is right now. How to change: make patching boring instead of preaching courage Don’t demand bravery from admins. Make patching boring, reversible, and career-safe. In my maturity post , I separated time cost from learning cost. Patch fear is unpaid learning cost. Here is how to address it: Shrink the unit of change. Monolithic “pet” servers breed fear. With immutable infrastructure, spin up patched containers, divert 5% of traffic, monitor telemetry, and flip over. Fast rollback eliminates deployment anxiety. This does not help with your 1987 enterprise database, however. Rehearse rollback. Teams fear deployment because rollback procedures are untested. If reverting an update is a single rehearsed action, bad vendor updates cause minor canary blips instead of emergency war rooms. Align metrics with error budgets. Stop measuring IT purely on uptime and Security purely on resolved CVEs. Adopt SRE-style error budgets where both teams co-own release currency and change-failure budgets. Ok, many of you will read the above 3 point and this “you Anton are such a PhD” here. A fair point, these are a bit theoretical, but to break out of a current pit we do need new theories too. Not just one more of “get the slaves to work faster” slogans. Patch faster, I mean :-) The lean team reality: two clocks instead of one But yes, on a more serious note : “Anton, we can’t rewrite our core monolith into immutable microservices by next quarter,” CISOs tell me. Fair! If you are stuck with fragile legacy systems, forcing 24-hour in-place patching may cause the very outage you fear. Instead, separate risk reduction from binary replacement and run two clocks: The Mitigation Clock (Fast): When touching the host server is high-risk, sever the attack path externally within hours using identity-aware proxies, micro-segmentation, host memory shielding, or WAF virtual patching. Note: a 15-minute mitigation clock that requires a two-hour emergency CAB meeting does not exist — pre-assign standing authority to pull the mitigation switch before the advisory drops. The Patch Clock (Measured): Deploy binary fixes through deployment rings at a pace supported by testing and rollback capabilities. Then tier it. Internet-exposed or known-exploited flaws get a verified mitigation within 24 hours and the patch as fast as the rings permit. Internal, segmented and well-monitored systems can let a patch soak for 7 to 14 days on a canary ring. Word of caution: not all mitigations survive a 14-day soak window. Payload-filtering virtual patches (WAF and IPS regexes) are blocklists that secretly relied on lazy attackers — against LLM-mutated exploits, they only buy hours. To buy days or weeks for your Patch Clock, favor structural mitigations (cutting network reachability, gating by identity, or disabling the vulnerable feature) that hold even when the payload mutates. Finally, track “ mitigation debt ”: set hard expiration dates and strip out temporary blocks once the patch lands, or “mitigated” will decay into permanent rule bloat and silent risk acceptance. Potentially useful actions based on this Five plays, after you stop scolding your sysadmins for caring about uptime: Calculate your internal patch failure rate. Measure how many security updates caused outages, rollbacks, or emergency re-patching over the past four quarters so your change-control debates run on your own telemetry, not folklore. Run a “Rollback Stopwatch Drill.” Pick a Tier-1 application and time how long it actually takes to revert a bad update in staging. If the answer is “restore from backup over six hours,” spend your engineering budget on one-click rollback before demanding faster patch SLAs. Split your vulnerability SLA into a Mitigation Clock and a Patch Clock. Require a verified compensating control within 24 hours for internet-exposed or actively exploited flaws — with pre-approved standing authority to deploy it — so binary fixes can move safely through canary rings. Re-verify patches for critical vulnerabilities (and retire mitigation debt). Continuously monitor KEV fixes post-deployment to catch the 2.3% of vendor patches that break or get bypassed within 90 days, and strip out temporary WAF or firewall blocks once a verified patch holds. Fix the blame physics with a shared change-failure budget. Agree in writing between Security and Infrastructure that a rehearsed, fast-rolled-back patch hiccup inside a canary ring is a celebrated pipeline catch, not a career-limiting outage. So, will we ever fear the exploit more than the patch? No! But honestly, we shouldn’t want operations teams to stop fearing production outages. An engineering org that doesn’t care if a Tuesday afternoon update takes down the hospital, the factory floor, or the billing gateway is a dangerous org. The goal in 2026 isn’t to breed fearless sysadmins who slap rushed vendor fixes onto fragile servers and pray. The goal is to build the rollback harnesses, canary rings, and structural mitigations so that fixing — or isolating — a flaw requires zero bravery at all. items.summary: "You can't outsource accountability". But it feels like that's what's happening when a disclosure notice refers to "an incident being at a third party", as though somehow that makes it better. It feels like the intent is to deflect responsibility , but ultimately, accountability remains with the party we entrusted our data to in the first place. It's also ultimately them who needs to decide whether to disclose the incident, so in the case of Optimizely this week, even though it's clearly their fault, it's up to the likes of Norwegian Airlines to decide whether they're contacting impacted individuals. And then, in their case, they haven't named the third party anyway! Strange times, I reckon.

items.title: OpenRouter Users’ Private AI Chats Possibly Exposed Via Compromised Third-Party Providers
items.summary: OpenRouter has removed three AI hosting providers and revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after researchers found evidence that some providers had been compromised or had failed to follow their data policies. In its November 22 incident notice , OpenRouter said it notified all potentially affected customers. The findings did not show a breach of OpenRouter itself, and the company did not say how many users or conversations may have been exposed. OpenRouter AI Chat Leaks OpenRouter gives customers a single API for accessing AI models hosted by different providers. But the company that first receives a request may not be the only one that handles it. If a provider forwards the request to another service, that service can also see the prompt. As Cyber Security News explained in its comparison of AI privacy gateways , routing requests and keeping them confidential are separate tasks. In its research report , Dragos said it sent nearly two million test prompts between July and November 2026. The prompts contained unique links and test credentials known as canary tokens. When a link was opened, or a credential was used, researchers could trace it to the original request. Dragos found evidence of compromises at three hosting providers. Some test requests were copied even though the model rejected them before processing. The researchers also saw signs that some requests marked for Zero Data Retention, a policy that says prompts and replies should not be stored, were kept or forwarded. In one case, a test link sent to a U.S. provider surfaced in a company chat in China 24 days later. What OpenRouter Users Should Check OpenRouter’s provider disclosures list notices from Novita, Phala, and Together. The company said it removed some endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility as a precaution, so the 125 removals do not represent 125 confirmed breaches. It is checking whether providers forward requests or replies to other companies and plans to verify endpoints before restoring their eligibility. Customers who received a notice should review what they sent through the affected provider. OpenRouter has removed three AI hosting providers and revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after researchers found evidence that some providers had been compromised or had failed to follow their data policies.

In its November 22 incident notice, OpenRouter said it notified all potentially affected customers. The findings did not show a breach of OpenRouter itself, and the company did not say how many users or conversations may have been exposed.

OpenRouter AI Chat Leaks

OpenRouter gives customers a single API for accessing AI models hosted by different providers. But the company that first receives a request may not be the only one that handles it.

If a provider forwards the request to another service, that service can also see the prompt. As Cyber Security News explained in its comparison of AI privacy gateways, routing requests and keeping them confidential are separate tasks.

In its research report, Dragos said it sent nearly two million test prompts between July and November 2026. The prompts contained unique links and test credentials known as canary tokens.

When a link was opened, or a credential was used, researchers could trace it to the original request. Dragos found evidence of compromises at three hosting providers. Some test requests were copied even though the model rejected them before processing.

The researchers also saw signs that some requests marked for Zero Data Retention, a policy that says prompts and replies should not be stored, were kept or forwarded. In one case, a test link sent to a U.S. provider surfaced in a company chat in China 24 days later.

OpenRouter’s provider disclosures list notices from Novita, Phala, and Together. The company said it removed some endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility as a precaution, so the 125 removals do not represent 125 confirmed breaches.

It is checking whether providers forward requests or replies to other companies and plans to verify endpoints before restoring their eligibility.

items.title: Hackers Could Execute Commands on WordPress, Email and Print Servers Through Upload2Shell Flaw
items.summary: A flaw in Ghostscript let researchers run commands on WordPress, Roundcube webmail, and Linux print servers through routine file processing. The vulnerability, dubbed Upload2Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-125396, affects upstream Ghostscript releases before 10.08.0. It sits in the software’s Type 1 font loader, but the affected servers did not need to expose Ghostscript directly. Their own preview, thumbnail, and print features delivered files to it. The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5 and lists a local attack vector. That describes the flaw at the interpreter level, not how a document arrives there. In research published on November 17, Paulos Yibelo and pwn.ai showed that network-facing services could pass remotely supplied files to the vulnerable code. The report describes research demonstrations, not confirmed attacks in the wild. Upload2Shell Bypassed Ghostscript’s Sandbox Ghostscript renders PDFs and PostScript documents. PostScript is a programming language for describing pages, so rendering a file means running instructions from it. Ghostscript’s -dSAFER mode is meant to limit what those instructions can access. Upload2Shell undermined those limits through a use-after-free, a memory flaw in which software keeps a reference to data after releasing the memory that held it. The font loader failed to check the type of data it received before an operation that could raise an error. That error exposed a protected write that document code was not supposed to control. Researchers used the resulting memory flaw to alter Ghostscript’s security checks while -dSAFER was still enabled. The test commands ran with the renderer’s permissions, not automatically as root. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of a separate Ghostscript PDF flaw , those permissions help determine what an attacker can reach after gaining code execution. WordPress, Roundcube and CUPS were Exposed On WordPress, the researchers reached Ghostscript through the media preview process on a site using Imagick and ImageMagick. The WordPress advisory tracks the core upload issue separately as CVE-2026-65640. It requires media upload privileges, which Authors and higher roles have by default. As covered in our WordPress Imagick vulnerability report , WordPress fixed that route in 7.0.4 and backported the fix, including to 6.9.7. The researchers also found that certain public upload features in Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor reached the renderer without a login in the configurations tested. On Roundcube 1.7.2, the sender needed no webmail account. The recipient had to view the message, but did not have to click or download the attachment. Roundcube’s server generated a thumbnail and passed the attachment through ImageMagick to Ghostscript. The test depended on an ImageMagick policy that allowed the handoff. The command ran as www-data , the web service account, rather than on the recipient’s device. The print server required no action from a recipient. On Debian 13, a shared CUPS queue accepted network print jobs without credentials and sent the test document to Ghostscript for conversion. The researchers confirmed command execution by writing a marker file as lp , the print service account. Requiring authentication blocked anonymous submission in the test, but did not repair the underlying flaw. These were three ways to reach the same vulnerable renderer, not three separate flaws in Ghostscript. Artifex fixed the underlying flaw in Ghostscript 10.08.0. Linux distributions can apply the same fix to an older release, so the upstream version number alone is not enough to judge exposure. Debian 13, for example, first shipped the fix in 10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u2 . Administrators should check their vendor’s package status for CVE-2026-125396 and verify the copy used by each service. Updating the host does not replace Ghostscript inside an existing container or application bundle. WordPress operators should apply both the core and renderer updates and review public forms that send uploads into the Media Library. If patching must wait, suspend automatic previews for untrusted files where practical. On print servers, require authentication for shared queues and restrict network access to them. Keep renderers isolated and give their service accounts only the access they need. The key check comes after a file is accepted. Storing a file did not start Ghostscript in the researchers’ tests. Rendering it did. Trace the worker that actually makes the preview, thumbnail or print output, then verify that worker uses the patched package. items.title: Hackers Exploit Microsoft Entra Connect Health Flaw to Access Admin Emails and Organization Data
items.summary: Attackers exploited a flaw in Microsoft Entra Connect Health to read administrator and technical contact email addresses, along with configuration data from affected organizations. A Microsoft customer notice shared on Reddit describes read-only access to those records, not access to inboxes or email messages. Microsoft fixed the flaw in its cloud service on November 19, 2026, and said customers do not need to install a patch. Microsoft said the vulnerability was introduced on July 23 and detected on November 9. Investigators reviewed service logs for unauthorized requests and concluded on November 20 that attackers had read tenant data. The flaw could also have allowed changes to monitoring settings, but Microsoft found none. The notice does not say when the unauthorized access began, who was behind it, or how many organizations were affected. Entra Connect Health Flaw Exposed Microsoft Entra Connect Health lets IT teams view alerts, performance data, and directory sync errors for identity systems running on their own servers. The flaw was in the cloud monitoring service’s API. Unlike a separate Entra ID flaw involving Global Administrator privileges , this incident involved confirmed reads of tenant records, with no reported takeover of administrator accounts through the flaw. The records included each affected tenant’s ID, display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope, and Entra license tier. They also showed whether directory sync was enabled, when it last ran, and whether the organization had set up Connect Health. The API still returned an expired certificate once used to register monitoring agents with an internal Microsoft service shut down in late 2024. Microsoft said the flaw did not expose passwords, password hashes, sign-in tokens, valid cryptographic keys, Azure subscription details, or details about how local Active Directory servers were arranged. The cloud fix stopped further access through the flaw, but it cannot take back the contact details already exposed. Knowing who administers a tenant and which domain it uses could make a fake support message more convincing. Previous Microsoft 365 phishing campaigns show why unexpected sign-in requests deserve scrutiny. The notice did not report any phishing linked to this incident. Microsoft advised organizations to alert their IT and security teams, confirm their technical contact details, and require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for privileged accounts. Where available, teams should use Privileged Identity Management to grant admin access only when needed. They should also check Connect Health settings and review Entra audit and sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for unexpected changes or unusual administrator activity. Administrators should open the Azure portal directly and check the security advisory in Azure Service Health to confirm whether it lists their tenant. The notice also points to Microsoft’s read-only GetTenant PowerShell script, which shows the types of records the API could have returned. It reports current values, so it cannot reconstruct what attackers saw or tell an organization which specific records were read. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? items.title: mass destruction of weapons
items.summary: There is a long history to chemical and biological warfare—one that, we at least hope, ended in 1993. The paucity of chemical and biological warfare today is a result of long-standing objections that culminated in the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention. It is striking that this formal end to most chemical weapons programs came within a year of the last US test of a nuclear weapon: similar sentiments, and a similar 1990s "end of history" context, motivated both. The similarity makes the differences more striking. Nuclear weapons are still part of the pop culture today, the quintessential "weapon of mass destruction" and a symbol of the destructive potential of modern warfare. But what of that term? Why "weapons of mass destruction?" The history of the phrase WMD is complex, and while it does predate nuclear weapons our modern use emerged in response to them. Still, it's a broader category. In today's language, WMD refers to nuclear, biological, or chemical weapons. Some of its most prominent invocations, namely in the Iraq War, referred to chemical rather than nuclear warfare. Still, to most Americans, chemical weapons are out of sight and out of mind. There are a few reasons: chemical weapons have been more or less prohibited in warfare for over one hundred years, so we have little experience with or memory of them. In fact, today, in the United States, there are none. That was the modern chemical war: the safe management, recovery, and destruction of an enormous stockpile of chemical weapons. This effort spanned military reservations across the United States, dismantling and burning chemical and biological munitions as life went on as usual outside of the fence. Well, at least, "as usual" for the Cold War: one of the effects of the stockpile was to maintain a sort of localized Cold War climate in those towns that fell downwind of it. Today, with the discovery of a dangerously poorly managed stockpile of Lead Azide that will require an exceptionally risky emergency measure to destroy, we are all acutely aware of the direction that the wind blows. The upcoming plume of lead over Iowa is far from the first time that dangerous compounds have blown away from military custody. There have been dozens of such incidents, with varying degrees of intentionality and risk to the public. Many were, at the time, classified. Others were simply covered up. While not exactly the future we wanted, it is perhaps a sign of progress that the upcoming detonation has been announced at all. The public notifications seem, to me, to be the result of an attitude shift that happened at the tail end of the era of US chemical warfare. Windblown plume forecasting models, originally developed for the fallout of nuclear war, were reapplied to risk analysis of chemical weapon stockpiles. The news was bad, so bad that civilian towns were hardened against attack: not enemy attack, but an attack of bad luck, an accident upwind. But first, we should consider how we got there. There are accounts of chemical and biological warfare dating to antiquity, although as with most early history it can be hard to tell what was speculative and what was actually done. By the 18th century, there had certainly been multiple uses of poisons and noxious chemicals on the battlefield. Chemical weapons in particular took a revolutionary step forward with the development of a more formal science of chemistry, during the 19th century. Several important advancements in chemistry occurred in the pursuit of poisonous gases, and just about every other advance in chemistry was applied to them. Still, even in this early era, there was more of an appetite for the development of chemical weapons than for their actual use. A particularly memorable incident in this history comes from Lyon Playfair, the very same who popularized the "Playfair Cipher" that makes a standard appearance in cryptography classes. In his role as a key scientific official during the Crimean War of the mid-1850s, he proposed the use of shells that would disperse a very poisonous form of Cyanide. Objections to the plan came not from pacifist do-gooders but from the weapons-builders themselves, who considered the whole thing morally questionable. Playfair's words in response are almost haunting in consideration of what would follow, outcomes of which he was simultaneously prescient and shockingly short-sighted. War is destruction, and the more destructive it can be made with the least suffering the sooner will be ended that barbarous method of protecting national rights. No doubt in time chemistry will be used to lessen the suffering of combatants, and even of criminals condemned to death. One of the reasons for the lackluster popularity of chemical weapons is that this notion of "easing the suffering" of the enemy, even if accepted as something other than madness, never really materialized. Particularly in the 1990s, the ethics of capital punishment in the United States came to be seen as sort of a technical problem. Maybe homicide by the state wasn't so bad if it was "painless," or "quick," or at least clinical in its appearance. The same idea pervaded chemical warfare in the 19th century, and in the 20th century it fell short in the same way that lethal injection has now. Objection to chemical weapons generally preceded their use. The Hague Convention of 1899 prohibited the form of chemical weapon that was then most obvious, the gas shell. That this prohibition applied specifically to artillery shells is significant: one of the complexities of chemical warfare is its interaction with domestic use. Like hollow-point bullets, tear gas, for example, is widely used in many nations' interiors—but it has been prohibited in warfare for many decades. This situation was already apparent with the first large-scale use of chemical weapons, at the onset of the First World War. Tear gas, a broad category of irritants that are not generally fatal but induce painful and disabling effects, was first developed in France. Parisian police struggled with organized criminal groups who would barricade themselves into buildings and successfully repel attempts at arrest. A commission was formed to investigate the matter in 1912, and it recommended the adoption of ethyl bromoacetate. Delivered to a barricaded position, it caused uncontrollable tearing, difficulty breathing, and considerable pain—enough to drive gangsters out of cover. That development in policing might have been controversial in its own right, but it was quickly overshadowed by the outbreak of the Great War. Tear gas was adapted to hand grenades, directed against the Germans at Alsace in 1914. In practice, this early chemical attack proved ineffective, but it opened Pandora's box. The Germans developed their own irritant shells, both sides justifying their use by leaning on the term "asphyxiating gas" in the Hague convention. Tear gases are unpleasant, but they are not asphyxiating as the term is defined. It was a slippery slope, though, and once the gears of war were in motion they would not be stopped. German chemists improved both the chemical agents and the means of delivery, such that during 1915 a drifting cloud of Chlorine gas was used to scatter French soldiers holding a defensive line. As it happened, the reticence of the Germans to march into their own poisonous cloud meant that they gained little advantage, but it proved the concept. Once again, the legality of the measure was questioned, but this time, the Germans emphasized the Hague convention's specific use of the word "shells"—no artillery shells having been involved in this particular weapon. Faced with this new threat, both sides developed countermeasures, and faced with those countermeasures, both developed new weapons. By the end of 1915 Phosgene was in wide use, and in 1917, the Germans introduced Mustard Gas. Mustard is a terrifying weapon, causing severe blistering of any exposed skin and extensive bleeding. Mustard Gas was extensively used by both sides, becoming part of routine infantry strategy, and along the way dooming tens of thousands of soldiers to a torturous ordeal in the overwhelmed military hospitals. Ironically, despite the extreme response it induced, Mustard Has was not particularly fatal. Many of its victims survived, disfigured after a long period of extreme suffering. These were the stories that came to be associated with chemical warfare. Far from Playfair's vision of "the least suffering," Mustard Gas became one of the war's main sources of it. Mustard-exposed soldiers convalescing in rows, their skin covered in blisters, their eyes sealed closed... these were the images that defined chemical warfare for decades to follow. While some use of chemical weapons continued after the First World War, Mustard Gas inspired a level of outrage that hung over the 1925 Geneva Conference. The Hague convention's prohibition on shells with asphyxiating gas was narrow enough that Mustard Gas arguably did not apply, so negotiators at Geneva agreed to stronger language. The Geneva Protocol, entering into force in 1928, broadly prohibited the use of chemical or biological agents in warfare between states. That could have been the end of the story. The Geneva Protocol was not perfectly observed, but it did prevent almost all use of such weapons. Despite significant technological advances made in Germany, including the development of several nerve agents during the 1930s, World War II elapsed with only limited use of chemical or biological weapons in combat. Most chemical attacks were by the Japanese, perhaps less affected by the experience of the First World War, and even then were directed mostly against other combatants in Asia. On the European front, only a handful of chemical attacks took place. Here, we arrive at the strangest contradiction in the history of chemical weapons: the near end of the use of chemical weapons, the Geneva Protocol, came before the peak of their development and manufacturing. Despite the limited chemical attacks during WWII, chemical weapons programs became larger than ever before. One reason was the Geneva Protocol's differentiation between combat use by state actors and other uses. To say that the Nazis made little use of chemical weapons, while correct in a certain technical sense, becomes absurd in the face of the Holocaust. Domestic use of chemical weapons only escalated, a dichotomy that still resonates today. This potential for domestic use or use against non-state adversaries (such as putting down revolutionary movements) justified a decision by most WWI combatants to continue development and manufacturing of chemical weapons. That created an ongoing possibility of their use, despite prohibition, which itself justified even more development. Consider the case of Australia, a nation that did not have a domestic chemical weapons program but still built massive stockpiles of imported chemical munitions during WWII. Why? For defense, of course: Australia was relatively close to Japan, the main chemical combatant, and felt the need to have a credible retaliation capability if Japan did decide to initiate all-out chemical war. This kind of reasoning, foreshadowing the doctrine that would demand nuclear weapons programs to the modern day, echoed around the world. Australia was importing those weapons principally from the US and UK, two countries that committed not to use chemical weapons, indeed never used them, and nevertheless operated major research centers and manufacturing plants throughout the war. The Germans clearly had a chemical inventory, which they so saliently demonstrated against their own population, and what if they decided to cast the treaty aside? Ought we to remain defenseless? The fear was not unfounded; Germany was known to have violated the Geneva Protocol on several occasions and some historians take the view that their use of chemical weapons was limited by technical issues rather than a policy decision. Churchill favored a chemical "first strike," although the suggestion didn't get much traction. In the US, as well, a notional retaliation capability was grounds for extensive R&D on rocket-delivered chemical warheads. Ironically, most of the US casualties to chemical weapons were self-inflicted. During the war the military manufactured stockpiles of Mustard Gas, Hydrogen Cyanide, and Cyanogen Chloride. These compounds were packaged into weapons and, in at least some cases, staged at the front in preparation for use. This program was a closely held secret and little is known of it even today. One major detail could not escape discovery: a German air raid on US Navy ships in Italy, in 1943, struck a ship carrying Mustard Gas. The resulting leakage at least contributed to the deaths of 69 people, and sickened hundreds. Already, perhaps the most dangerous thing about chemical weapons was possessing them. Chemical warfare programs only accelerated after WWII. The newly developed German nerve agents, including Sarin 1 , made it to the US as spoils of war. The research programs that formed around these new agents are some of the most infamous of the period, including exposure of thousands of soldiers to small doses of poisons to observe the effects, a program that continued at Edgewood Arsenal in Maryland until the public became aware—and the program collapsed in scandal—in 1975. The involvement of LSD in these experiments often sees them lumped together with MKULTRA, but the vast majority of the research was on less exotic substances: VX, Sarin, Mustard Gas, Tear Gas. Edgewood was also the manufacturing center for Mustard and Phosgene. What Edgewood couldn't provide was storage; it didn't have room for the well-separated bunkers required for munitions. The Army built new installations for the stockpile: Redstone Arsenal in Alabama, Rocky Mountain Arsenal in Colorado, Pine Bluff Arsenal in Arkansas, and Tooele Ordnance Depot in Utah. At each of these sites, hundreds of acres of earth-covered concrete sheds stored weapons at a distance that wouldn't set off their neighbors. In the very early years of the Cold War, the US Army weaponized a new chemical agent called BZ. BZ gained notoriety because of its psychological effects, which included hallucinations, and because of various accusations that it was covertly used by the US during the 1960s. These allegations don't generally hold up, but they illustrate the atmosphere of paranoia that chemical weapons created, and in response to which more chemical weapons were developed. BZ was produced at Swannanoa, North Carolina, and assembled into weapons at Pine Bluff Arsenal, where binary (two parts that are mixed together) nerve agents were produced as well. Phosphate was manufactured at Muscle Shoals, Alabama, and VX at Newport, Indiana. The Aberdeen Proving Ground handled Mustard gas manufacturing and filling. The Rocky Mountain Arsenal, though, just outside of Denver, was the center of the post-war program: Sarin, Mustard, and Sulfur Mustard were all produced and stored there. The Vietnam War proved a pivotal conflict for chemical warfare, as with so many other aspects of military history. Defoliants, such as Agent Orange, were not considered to be chemical weapons and saw heavy use in Vietnam. While targeted at plants, they were not safe for humans either, and played a major role in creating a generation of disabled veterans. In the meantime, the accidental dangers became more apparent: in 1968, an accident at Dugway Proving Ground in Utah released the nerve gas VX and killed thousands of sheep. The Army denied involvement, and then later admitted involvement but denied fault, a position it maintained into the '90s. Despite attempts to maintain secrecy, the Dugway sheep incident brought public attention to the chemical weapons program—which had maintained such a low profile that many didn't realize it existed. Press investigations after Dugway revealed further problems: disposal practices that had released large quantities of chemical agents into the ocean, handling accidents in overseas military installations, and of course numerous human experiments that fell far short of the ethical standards of the time. In short, the Dugway incident reminded the public, and Congress, that the US Army Chemical Corps existed. It had thousands of soldiers, dozens of facilities, and maintained an inventory of chemical weapons that spanned a national network of ammunition igloos. Ongoing manufacturing operations in the 1960s included BZ cluster bombs, VX shells, Hydrogen Cyanide, and others. Once the press latched on to the program, though, it was the beginning of the end. In 1969, President Nixon announced a "no first use" policy for chemical weapons and the complete prohibition of biological weapons—a stronger policy than has been adopted for nuclear weapons even to this day. As part of the 1969 declaration, Nixon also ended the biological weapons program entirely. I have not spoken as much of biological weapons here, as the scale of the US effort was always smaller than that for chemical agents, but I shouldn't understate it. A half dozen viral and bacterial infections, including Anthrax and Botulism, were weaponized in research laboratories. In part because of moral and practical concerns in the military, most of these were never manufactured at scale and delivery systems (such as artillery shells or warheads) were rarely developed to maturity. When Nixon ordered the program ended, its small scale made it relatively straightforward to destroy stockpiled material. Much of the laboratory-scale work was retained, anyway, for its value in researching defensive measures. Chemical weapons were a different matter entirely, because of the scale of the stockpiles. Continuing expansion of the chemical weapons program saw new stockpiles at Umatilla, Oregon; Pueblo, Colorado; Hawthorne, Nevada; Anniston, Alabama; and Blue Grass, Kentucky. At the peak, the United States disclosed an inventory of 31,100 metric tons of nerve agents and Mustard, stored across a dozen sites. Nearly half was concentrated in Tooele, Utah. Due to the old age of many chemical munitions, there had already been efforts to dispose of aged-out stockpiles in the 1960s. This program took the crude form of missions like "Operation CHASE," or "Cut Holes and Sink 'Em," in which Liberty ships full of munitions were towed off of the coast of Florida and scuttled. Only some carried chemical weapons, but well-founded concerns over the environmental impacts of such a chemical assault on the ocean led to legislation prohibiting this means of disposal in 1972. Other smaller-scale disposal efforts had taken forms like loading Phosphorus into barrels, rolling them into a lake, and then shooting at them until they sank, but besides the generally crude nature of this approach there were only so many lakes that could be so used. Congress had intervened in other ways, as well. Starting in 1970, the Office of the Surgeon General was tasked with reviewing the way that chemical weapons were handled and destroyed. This responsibility shifted around several agencies, ultimately involving the Centers for Disease Control, and brought a level of visibility into chemical weapons management that forced the Department of Defense to take a far more systematic and cautious approach to the remaining stockpile. During the 1970s, the Army's Chemical Corps took on a new focus: safe handling and disposal. The most concerning—and contentious—part of the stockpile was weapons that had been "forward staged" in Europe and Asia. These were intended to allow a fast retaliation to any chemical attack on Europe, but by this point they had become unpopular with host nations like Germany and Japan. This set up the first wave of chemical demilitarization: a months-long Army/Navy effort moved the chemical inventory from Okinawa, thousands of tons of munitions with nerve agents and Mustard Gas, to Johnston Atoll. While better known for its role in the nuclear weapons program, Johnston also served as a base for satellite programs (both intelligence collection and anti-satellite weapons) and a test site for biological and chemical weapons. Starting in 1971, storage and destruction of chemical weapons was made the installation's main purpose. In reaction to the safety incidents of the late '60s, legislation passed in the early 1970s that prohibited transfer of most chemical weapons from overseas to the United States. Instead, over the following decades, nearly all US chemical weapons that had been stored outside of North America were consolidated to Johnston Atoll. The inventory there in the 1990s included even German-made chemical shells that had been captured by the Allies and stored in Germany for study. In 1972, an Army command was formally established to manage the destruction of chemical weapons. The first priority was made the M34 cluster bomb. Designed in the 1950s, the M34 was the first Cold War-era chemical weapon and already considered obsolete. M34s were among the weapons destroyed by ocean disposal during Operation CHASE, but that method had since been prohibited. The Army had to find another way to handle more than 20,000 M34 bombs still stored by Denver, and because of the location of the weapons that method would have to actually neutralize the agents. For the Sarin-laden M34s, a hole was carefully drilled to drain the Sarin from each of the "bomblets" that made up the cluster munition. That Sarin liquid was then mixed with a neutralizing caustic chemical in a sealed reaction chamber. The resulting salt brine was dried, and the precipitated solids (no longer a nerve agent but still an environmental toxin) were buried in nearly 20,000 steel drums. In the meantime, Rocky Mountain Arsenal burned tens of thousands of tons of Mustard gas projectiles in an on-site incinerator, and began chemical neutralization of outdated VX munitions that had been relocated to the site for storage. These early disposal operations at Rocky Mountain Arsenal took place in part because of its proximity to a major city, and a political factor that had made it the top priority for site closure. That was also a liability: disposal operations added to existing environmental contamination, exacerbating a groundwater plume that killed nearby crops and creating a new set of toxic landfills. The weapons that were destroyed there in the '60s and '70s were the easy cases, intact weapons with chemical agents that had known neutralization techniques or were easily incinerated. The Army realized that many other chemical weapons, including older weapons that were already in poor condition and beginning to leak, would require a more complex approach with greater risk of exposure. To develop these techniques, the Chemical Corps established the Chemical Agent Munitions Disposal System (CAMDS) at the Deseret Chemical Depot, a new purpose-built installation adjacent to the Tooele Army Depot on the south side of the Great Salt Lake. CAMDS became the primary R&D site for disposal, and pioneered techniques that included robotic remote handling, semi-automated processing lines, and high-temperature incineration with extensive filtration and chemical treatment of the exhaust. Over the lifespan of CAMDS, more than 91 tons of chemical agents were treated, but most operations at CAMDS served as pilots for larger-scale facilities at other installations. In 1981, an ambitious construction program started at Johnston Atoll: the Johnston Atoll Chemical Agent Disposal System (JACADS). Based on techniques in use at CAMDS and built over five years, JACADS then went through four years of testing and validation before the first full-scale chemical weapons disposal line started operation in 1990. Nerve gas shells were carefully unloaded from storage pallets and set up on a belt. That carried them through a sort of de-production line, where the shells were opened, drained, and washed. The explosives and chemicals they contained were burned in a high-temperature incinerator, while the metal casings of the shells and other components were treated in a high-temperature kiln to ensure they were safe to handle. Simultaneously, a set of "auxiliary" incinerators and kilns processed packaging materials and handling waste. Monitoring systems continuously sampled emissions for any escaping chemical weapons, and periodically such leaks were discovered. This period of chemical weapons history is an odd one, because the political tide had turned against chemical weapons but the Army's inertia continued in the direction of chemical warfare. As JACADS was under construction, the Army built a set of new manufacturing plants at Pine Bluff Arsenal. This would specifically produce binary chemical weapons, which use two separate agents that are relatively safe until they are mixed to produce a nerve agent. Binary weapons can be much safer to handle, since the mixing doesn't occur until an in-flight "arming" stage. They were also seen as an escalation in chemical warfare, especially in the context of the Cold War. As often happens with controversial weapons systems, the Army's work to productionize binary weapons was also their undoing. Controversy around the new weapon designs, and the facilities for manufacturing them, led to a renewal in negotiations with the Soviet Union for some type of chemical weapons treaty. Domestically, the issue made its way to Washington, where in 1986 legislation passed requiring that all non-binary (and thus less safe to handle) weapons be safely destroyed. Lack of congressional enthusiasm (resulting in limited funding), the intrinsic complexity of safely handling dangerous chemicals and explosives, and standard military acquisition problems meant that the new binary weapons programs were slow in coming. Despite the start of construction on several binary weapons plants in 1982, only one was operational by the 1990s, producing the M20 and M21 cartridges which produced Sarin upon mixing in an artillery shell. Barely after M20/M21 production started, ongoing talks with the Soviet Union led to an early agreement to end chemical weapons production—a somewhat informal memorandum, but one that kickstarted negotiations for a formal treaty, complete with timelines and verification requirements. In 1991, Congress ordered the destruction of all material related to the chemical weapons program. This included binary materials, as well as waste, experimental samples, and chemical weapons waste buried in landfills. The United States had, at that point, officially ended its chemical weapons program—a position that would be reinforced by the 1997 ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention, a complete demilitarization treaty with nearly every nation of the world, and most critically key opponent Russia, as signatories. In a certain strategic sense, the US was no longer a "chemical power," the entire stockpile considered retired. In a practical sense, there were still thousands of tons of chemical agents, packaged into hundreds of thousands of tons of munitions, stored in concrete bunkers from Alabama to Oregon. Throughout the last decade of that century, every chemical weapon storage site became a disposal operation. Congressional restrictions and political realities meant that chemical weapons could not generally be transported between sites. During the 1980s, Sarin-carrying Mk 116 "Weteye" bombs stored at Rocky Mountain Arsenal were dismantled there until safety concerns forced a decision to discontinue demilitarization operations at the edge of a major city. The remaining stockpile at Denver was small, but still included almost a thousand Weteye bombs, particularly the "difficult cases" that had begun to leak. The decision was made to ship these bombs to Tooele for safer storage and disposal at the planned CAMDS. The move did happen, but not without inspiring one of the largest political battles of the chemical weapons era, a media circus that considerably frayed relations between the Army and the state of Utah. Congress followed up by restricting domestic transportation, and by the time disarmament was fully underway it was clear that it would all need to be done "as is, where is." I put a lot of time into writing this, and I hope that you enjoy reading it. If you can spare a few dollars, consider supporting me on ko-fi . You'll receive an occasional extra, subscribers-only post, and defray the costs of providing artisanal, hand-built world wide web directly from Albuquerque, New Mexico. The US Army Chemical Demilitarization and Remediation Activity built the Tooele Chemical Agent Disposal Facility (scaled up from CAMDS), Anniston CADF, Umatilla CADF, and Newport CADF. Failures of several pilot programs to develop a practical alternative to high-temperature incineration led to the construction of the Aberdeen and Pine Bluff CADFs shortly after. Manufacturing facilities were converted, sometimes hastily, to dismantling facilities. The Chemical Weapons Convention's verification scheme started a comprehensive audit of military stockpiles, with storage sites physically searched for chemical inventory. A dream that seems so remote for nuclear weapons had been achieved: it was now military policy, and a major military objective, to find and destroy every last chemical weapon. At the turn of the millennium, JACADS completed its mission, having incinerated nearly half a million weapons—6% of the total US stockpile—stored at Johnston Atoll. Disposal facilities were operating at nearly every stockpile site, almost exclusively by incineration, although some neutralization operations continued at smaller scale. While most of the chemical inventory took the form of large quantities of finished weapons at depots, there was also a sort of "miscellaneous" category. Smaller supplies of weapons that had been moved for testing or R&D, stored agents that were never assembled into weapons, laboratory samples and waste, and other "etcetera" cases made up the category of "non-stockpile" chemical materials. For example, the military had manufactured over a hundred thousand "chemical agent identification sets," sort of portable laboratories and field guides for soldiers that might encounter chemical weapons in the field. These contained small samples of several chemical weapons, and were stored at several sites. They met their end via the Rapid Response System, a three-semi-trailer portable agent disposal facility that could perform a range of neutralization processes at small scale. After qualification testing at Tooele, the Rapid Response System made a sort of nationwide tour of each facility. A particularly hard case were those weapons that had begun to leak, or where the explosives had become unstable. These were dangerous to handle or transport, even over short distances. In response, Sandia National Laboratories developed the Explosive Destruction System. The EDS was a single semi trailer, but one that traveled with about a dozen supporting trucks. It was typically set up under a tent with a negative pressure air filtration system and an airlock for entry. Chemical munitions were set up in a tray, and shaped explosive charges placed across the top. This nightmare casserole is then loaded into a huge steel chamber, where the explosives are detonated to both "open" the weapons and thermally neutralize some of the contents. The rest of the chemical agent is destroyed by neutralizing chemicals injected into the chamber post-detonation, and the steel vessel is heated and rotated to mix everything up and complete the operation. During the '90s and '00s, multiple EDS units were used to handle small inventories of "discovered" chemical weapons, leaking and damaged weapons, and non-stockpile materials. After the Chemical Weapons Convention, the EDS convoy included a "treaty trailer" where staff from the international treaty enforcement body Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) independently observed the work. Major storage sites required industrial-scale facilities. At Umatilla, 1,000 concrete bunkers held artillery shells, rockets, bombs, landmines, sprayers, and storage containers. These weapons contained nerve agents Sarin and VX, as well as Mustard Gas and blister agents. 1980s upgrades to the facility included better sealing the igloos, fitting them with drains that would contain water from the bunkers for sampling, and adding air filtration on the bunker vents. These reduced the risk from leaking weapons, but as the stockpile aged, leakage was a more and more serious problem. Starting in 1998 the Army carefully recorded each leak; prior to that year most went unnoticed. Environmental personnel interviewed former employees and found multiple stories of leaks, cracks, and other incidents. In at least one case, a leaking munition described by a former worker was found, still stored, right in the bunker where he said it had sprayed its contents across the wall. Contracted to Raytheon, construction of the Umatilla Chemical Agent Disposal Facility (UMCDF) began in 1997. The plant went in to operation in 2004. With 819 miles of wire, 25,000 cubic yards of concrete, and 2,655 tons of steel, the Army boasted that it was "among the most advanced industrial facilities in the world." Destroying the full inventory at Umatilla would take years. A risk-prioritized approach was used in which large-quantity nerve agent weapons were destroyed first, and the relatively less dangerous munitions (such as those with only Mustard Gas or those with very small quantities of nerve agent) were left for later. Operated by contractor URS, the UMCDF consisted of a Container Handling Building where airtight, double-walled steel containers that had been packed and sealed in the bunkers were inspected and transferred to conveyors. From that point, they moved into the Munitions Demilitarization Building where the containers were opened, munitions were disassembled and drained, and the chemical agents and components were delivered to various incinerators. While a few workers with extensive protective equipment performed the most complex disassembly tasks, most operations within the Demilitarization Building were performed by a system of conveyors, hoists, and robots under remote control. Different components went into different incinerators. Liquid from washing weapons and containers went to the Liquid Incinerators, where it was mixed with air and natural gas and fed into a two-stage vortex burner system operating between 2,500 and 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,370-1,480 C). Explosives and propellants, usually contaminated by residual chemical agents, went to the Deactivation Furnace System. A 32 foot long rotating drum kiln treated the waste at a minimum of 1,100 degrees Fahrenheit (590 C) for 7-10 minutes, followed by a discharge conveyor that kept them nearly as hot for another 15 minutes. Most of the material burned during this process, leaving ash (packaged for disposal in a chemical landfill) and flue gas that passed through a final stage of incineration in an afterburner chamber. Just about everything else, mostly the metal casings and components of weapons, went to the Metal Parts Furnace (MPF). The MPF was a three-stage incinerator, with a system of belts and airlocks to move material through it in an almost continuous stream. The three stages held materials for various time periods (depending on the type of waste) at temperatures from 1,450 F to 1,800 F (790 C to 980 C), until the materials arrive in the out-feed airlock where they are cooled. The air blown in for cooling was sampled on the way out and tested to ensure that it was free of chemical agents. All gases from the MPF were processed by a multi-stage afterburner incinerator. The UMCDF required an array of support facilities, like the Pollution Abatement System that received the exhaust gases from all of the incinerators. This exhaust, clean of chemical agents but still bearing a variety of interesting and toxic chemicals, was cooled in a quench tower and then put through a series of chemical scrubbers and filters before a final incinerator stage for good measure. Liquid brines, collected from the scrubber towers and parts of the Demilitarization Building process, went to a treatment plant where the water was evaporated off (and the vapors scrubbed) to leave dry crystallized salts. These were packaged for disposal at a hazardous waste landfill. Laboratory, utility, and office buildings made up the rest of the complex. Congressional scrutiny of chemical weapons also led to the Chemical Stockpile Emergency Preparedness Program. This legislation responded to accidents that had occurred at storage and demilitarization sites by requiring that the Army and FEMA take measures to protect nearby communities. The highest population concentration around a major depot, after the relatively early end of operations at Rocky Mountain Arsenal, was found in Oregon and Washington towns around Umatilla. In that region, FEMA funded the construction of a new emergency operations center, installation of sirens, and positive-pressure chemical filtration systems on schools. It was projected that residents of Umatilla would have to move into sealed shelter in less than an hour, were there to be an accident at the depot. A FEMA-funded computer modeling system, at the Emergency Operations Center, would project plume travel to inform evacuation and shelter decisions. The counties stockpiled protective suits and other equipment, and arranged military training on surviving chemical attack for firefighters. By 2000, residents of the area were provided with "tone alert" radios to sound an alarm in their home. Counties distributed "shelter in place kits," with tape and plastic sheeting, to offer residents something to do if the radios ever did sound. The East Oregonian described a county official saying that the kits wouldn't really seal a room, but "may buy more time for a family inside." Pressurization systems were made standard in new schools in the area, and added to the hospital and a nursing home in Umatilla. Working with the CDC, the State of Oregon trained medical personnel on chemical weapons response and distributed the nerve agent antidote Atropine to hospitals. FEMA funds were directed to school districts to buy more buses—a local transportation capability that could be conscripted for an evacuation. In 2008, the last nerve gas weapon, a VX land mine, passed through the plant. The last Mustard Gas weapon was processed in 2011, and evacuation sirens sounded their last Tuesday test. In 2013, the Army published a plan to remediate contamination at Umatilla, demolish the plant, and return the land to other use. Even this process was complex: many of the bunkers were contaminated and had to be carefully cleaned. Much of the demolition debris from the incinerator plant had to be handled as hazardous waste. Each and every bunker was swabbed for testing, soil samples were taken, buildings were knocked over and covered. At the building where workers changed into their protective equipment, septic leachate and dryer lint were collected as chemical waste. In 2023, the Army transferred the 9,511 acres that made up the installation to a coalition of local governments. Much of it will be used by the Oregon National Guard as a training site, other areas are slated to become industrial parks, and the tribal government of the Cayuse, Umatilla, and Walla Walla peoples will operate a large area as an environmental preserve—some of which will require an ongoing program of monitoring and institutional controls. The last chemical weapons in the US stockpile were located at Blue Grass Army Depot, where the Blue Grass Chemical Agent Disposal Facility processed the final Sarin-filled M55 rocket on July 7th, 2023—just ahead of the September 30th deadline set by the Chemical Weapons Convention. Measured from Congress's 1986 legislative mandate, the complete destruction of the US inventory of chemical and biological weapons took 37 years. Closure of the later disposal facilities is still ongoing, and the small-scale portable disposal systems will be retained for use on any chemical or biological weapons that might turn up in the future. An Assistant Secretary of Defense, Deborah Rosenblum, said that "this achievement demonstrates our credibility to the international community and has helped move the US government toward closing this particular chapter of US military history." There are few chapters of military history that ever close. The arc of the chemical weapons program, developed under wartime pressures but accelerated during the curious pressure of the Cold War, largely rejected by both the military and the public, and then wrapped up under international agreement at great expense... it is impossible not to compare it to that of the nuclear weapons program. Negotiations with the Soviet Union leading to a bilateral agreement, followed by an international convention, to completely disarm: the dream of generations of nuclear weapons protestors. It seems so far away, so impossible, for nuclear weapons that it's hard to remember that we've done it once before. So why can't we do it again? Well, the comparison isn't entirely fair. For one, the strategic significance of chemical weapons has never been on par with that of their nuclear peers. The story of World War I shows that chemical weapons are hard to use effectively outside of a few very specific situations, and that never really changed. They have a small area of effect, making them useful mostly to clear the way to advance, but they poison the land such that they can prevent that advance actually happening. Chemical disarmament was achieved, in good part, because the chemical weapons just weren't that important to begin with. One also wonders if the history of use is a factor: chemical weapons were widely used in the First World War, which both spread awareness of their horrific effects and made them more approachable, more understandable, as a part of combat. Nuclear weapons have seen such limited use that they remain more of a symbol than a real weapon, surrounded by such a mystique that their power seems both unlimited and unlikely to actually matter. During the 1899 Hague Convention, which banned the use of "shells containing asphyxiating gas," there was a sole vote against. That vote came from the United States, through its representative, Captain Alfred Mahan of the Navy. He explained his vote thus: The inventiveness of Americans should not be restricted in the development of new weapons. We do consider ourselves to be a powerful culture. The development and manufacturing of chemical weapons was a massive program, involving tens of thousands of workers across the military and private industry. The dismantling of those same weapons happened on the same scale, and often faced even more formidable technical challenges. Perhaps our inventiveness could be less restricted in the destruction of weapons, as well. German researchers gave nerve agents names such as Sarin and Tabun, while the US and NATO used two-letter codes like GB and GA. In fact, these are the same: Sarin is GB and Tabun is GA. I find the acronyms difficult to remember, and the German names are generally the ones used in popular media, so I use the German names when applicable. The problem is that nerve agents developed within NATO countries, such as VX, have no such names. The result will unfortunately be a mix of both conventions. ↩
